title: African, Haitian and Caribbean roots of the beat
summary: Cahn sees Indian music as a base for New Orleans music, via Africa, Haiti and Santo Domingo; a Paul Oliver Africa field recording is played.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Do you see this as a, this type of music, the street music, or as a base for other types of music that were made here?

I think it's, it takes its base or is the base for a lot of New Orleans music. You'll find that the beat is very similar. It comes possibly from Africa through Santa Domingo and Haiti up, up to New Orleans. And there's no question in my mind that it was part of the slave music back in the 1850s or the 1830s.
So you would think it would definitely.
It was definitely, very definitely. It has been influenced by the music that has come over.
In 1965, I think it was Paul Oliver, the English researcher, did a trip to Africa. And this is the music that he recorded when he did his field research.
And this is the music that he recorded when he did his field research. Song Song Yeah, come on. Yeah.
Jules sounds very similar to the Monterey Indians, don't you think?

Very similar. So again, I think a piece of evidence to prove maybe some origin. Definitely there were some, there were a African or through Latin influence, Latin and African influence in the music which the Indians have done.

I would say that the influence is principally what we would call Afro-Cubanen or the Haitian or from Santa Domingo. We had a large influx coming into Santa Domingo, from Santa Domingo to Louisiana, especially in the sugar plantation life, which undoubtedly brought the language and the rhythm and everything that goes with all of the goodies.
